newsitem.title: POLAND: Workers briefly strike against Polish oil sell-off.
newsitem.headline: Workers briefly strike against Polish oil sell-off.

text.p: Workers of Poland's large state-owned petrol distribution company CPN SA staged a two-hour warning strike on Wednesday to protest against the government's plan to restructure and privatise the oil sector.

Protesters idled CPN's fuel storage centres and road and rail tanker transport but the company's nearly 1,400 filling stations operated normally, said Zdzislaw Kedzierski, chairman of the CPN Workers Trade Union.
"We demand talks with the government... If our demands are ignored we will step up our protest action, which could involve an indefinite strike," Kedzierski told Reuters.
CPN workers are protesting against the government's plan to divide their company into three firms as part of the oil sector transformation programme.

Under the plan, the fuels storage centres (Naftobazy) and the tank transport company (DEC) are to be carved out from CPN and remain in the state's hands for some time, while the leaner CPN will be partially sold off along with the refineries.

CPN workers, who under the privatisation law will be entitled to 15 percent of their firm's shares for free when the company is sold, say the value of the shares will fall dramatically after the company's division.
Kedzierski said the unions also feared the division of CPN could cost the jobs of 4,500 of the company's 14,000 workers.
Officials were not immediately available for comment on how the government would respond to the dispute.

The CPN protest has delayed the implementation of the oil sector sell-off programme by postponing the allocation of the the company's shares to Nafta Polska SA, a company set up last year to oversee the scheme.

Nafta Polska has already been given shares of Poland's seven refineries, including two large one in the cities of Plock and Gdansk, and plans to invite bids for 20-30 percent stakes in them. The stakes could later be extended.
CPN shares are to go to Nafta directly and to Nafta-controlled refineries so that investors buying into them would also gain access to the distributor's lucrative network of filling stations.
But many analysts say that foreign investors would not be keen on buying the refineries without guarantees that they would take over part of CPN's retail chain at the same time.

They say that only foreign investors can provide about $3 billion which Poland's oil sector needs over the next several years to face foreign competition after the planned lifting of trade barriers protecting the industry.
